title: SYSK Selects: How Tea Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Tea Works." Chuck introduces it as a Saturday pick from March 2015. The hosts cover the types of tea (green, black, oolong, white, yellow) and their common origin in the Camellia sinensis plant, legends of Emperor Shennong, the spread of tea through the Tang dynasty, Japan's tea ceremony, the Dutch and Portuguese introduction of tea to Europe, Catherine of Braganza, the East India Company and Indian tea cultivation, tea clippers, the British tea tax and smuggling, and the Boston Tea Party. They explain how tea is harvested and processed (withering, rolling, oxidation, drying, sorting; steaming for green tea), differences between loose leaf and bagged tea, brewing temperatures and steep times, matcha preparation, iced tea's origin at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, caffeine levels, antioxidants and the free radical theory of aging, and a listener mail segment about left-handedness. Includes a brief ad-free tangent about coffee and the USDA.

segments.title: Rerun intro and tea banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as a Saturday select from March 2015. The hosts chat about their tea preferences, including green, English breakfast, Earl Grey, oolong and herbal teas, and clarify that all true teas come from one plant.

segments.title: Legend of Emperor Shennong and early tea history
segments.summary: The hosts recount the legend of Emperor Shennong, who reportedly drank water into which leaves blew, and discuss tea's use in the Zhou and Han dynasties and its spread under the Tang dynasty.

segments.title: Tea in Japan and the tea ceremony
segments.summary: Tea spread to Japan through priests studying in China, and the Japanese developed the tea ceremony. The hosts discuss its ritual nature and the concept of ichi go ichi e.

segments.title: Tea arrives in Europe and England
segments.summary: Portuguese and Dutch traders brought tea to Europe in the seventeenth century, and Catherine of Braganza's tea drinking helped popularize it in England. The East India Company's end of its China trade monopoly in 1834 led to Indian tea cultivation and the first Darjeeling auction in Britain in 1839.

segments.title: Tea clippers, Boston Tea Party and British tea tax
segments.summary: After the monopoly ended, tea clipper ships raced home to London from China. The hosts also cover the Boston Tea Party, the British tea tax that lasted until 1964, and widespread tea smuggling in the late eighteenth century.

segments.title: Tea types and the harvesting process
segments.summary: The hosts explain that all teas come from the same plant and differ by processing. Tea is mostly hand-harvested, typically the top two leaves and bud, and the leaves begin oxidizing once picked.

segments.title: How black, green and oolong tea are made
segments.summary: The hosts describe the black tea process of withering, rolling (orthodox or CTC), oxidation, drying and sorting. They then cover green tea, which is steamed to stop oxidation, and oolong, which is partly oxidized and partly steamed.

segments.title: White tea, herbal tisanes and matcha
segments.summary: White tea is picked only two days a year and is less grassy. The hosts note that chai, chamomile and rooibos are not true teas, and they discuss matcha, its shade-grown powdered preparation, and its L-theanine content.

segments.title: Brewing tea, loose leaf vs bagged, and iced tea
segments.summary: The hosts cover brewing temperatures and steep times for each tea type and compare loose leaf with bagged tea. They then explain iced tea's origin at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair.

segments.title: Health benefits, antioxidants and caffeine
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the free radical theory of aging, antioxidants in tea such as catechins, correlations with health benefits that are not proven, and caffeine levels compared with coffee.

segments.title: Listener mail on left-handedness
segments.summary: Listeners write about being forced to use their right hand as children. The hosts read the mail and invite future topic suggestions.
